name: Ron Ligero
description: The Cuban style, codified in the 1860s when Facundo Bacardí filtered and aged his rum into something light enough for a mixed drink. Every clean, dry white rum in the world descends from that decision.
funFact: Cuban law requires even white rum to be aged and then filtered back to clarity, so the colourless bottle in front of you has still spent time in oak.

serve.how: This is a mixing rum by design. A daiquiri with lime and sugar, or a mojito, is what it was built for. Neat, the aged expressions are dry and elegant, but the white is not meant to be sipped.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented, column-distilled, aged and charcoal-filtered.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, to a light spirit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years even for white, then filtered clear

composition.process: Filtering after ageing removes the colour but leaves the softness, which is the whole trick of the Cuban style.

name: Rhum Barbancourt
description: Haitian rum made from fresh cane juice and distilled twice in the Charentais method its founder brought from Cognac in 1862. It sits between agricole and Caribbean rum and belongs entirely to neither.
funFact: Dupré Barbancourt was a Frenchman from the Charente who applied cognac's double pot distillation to Haitian cane, a method the distillery still uses.

serve.how: Neat or over a single cube for the aged expressions, which have real cocoa and dried fruit depth. The younger bottling makes an exceptional daiquiri, since the cane juice base brings grass the molasses rums lack.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented and double pot-distilled, then oak-aged.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Charentais double distillation in copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Limousin oak, four to fifteen years

composition.process: Double pot distillation is a cognac technique, and it gives a rounder spirit than the single-column agricole method.

name: Mamajuana
description: A Dominican bottle packed with tree bark, roots and herbs, filled with rum, red wine and honey, and left to steep. Taíno in origin, spiked with European ingredients after contact, and credited locally with curing everything.
funFact: The Taíno originally drank the herb infusion as a tea; rum and wine were added after the Spanish arrived, and the bottle has been refillable ever since.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, and the bottle keeps going: when it empties you top it up with more rum and let it steep again. The first fill is the harshest, and it improves for years afterwards.

composition.summary: Bark, roots and herbs steeped in rum, red wine and honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Dominican rum, with red wine and honey

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bejuco bark, anise, star anise, agave, cinnamon and a dozen more

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused only; the bottle is refilled repeatedly

composition.process: The dry bark is cured first with rum that is then discarded, since the first extraction is bitter and harsh.

name: Barbados Rum
description: Pot and column stills blended together to a balance nobody else quite matches, from the island that has the strongest claim to inventing rum in the 1650s. Elegant where Jamaica is loud.
funFact: Mount Gay holds a deed from 1703, which makes it the oldest rum brand still in production anywhere in the world.

serve.glass: Rocks glass with one large cube
serve.how: Neat or over a single cube for the aged bottlings. The balance of pot and column makes it the most versatile rum on the shelf: good enough to sip, characterful enough to hold up in a Daiquiri or a Rum Old Fashioned.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented and distilled in both pot and column stills, then blended.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot and twin-column, blended together

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Tropical ageing in ex-bourbon oak, two years and up

composition.process: Blending the two still types is the house method, and the ratio is what defines each distillery's style.

name: Trinidad Rum
description: Light, dry column-still rum, cleaner and less sweet than most of the Caribbean, and shaped by a distillery better known for its bitters. Trinidad rum is the quiet workhorse of the region.
funFact: Angostura's distillery produces both the island's rum and the bitters, though the bitters recipe uses no Angostura bark and never has.

serve.how: Neat or over ice. The dryness makes it a good rum for anyone who finds Caribbean rum too sweet, and it holds its shape in a Rum Punch better than richer styles do.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented and column-distilled to a light spirit, then aged.
composition.process: Distilling to a high strength strips out congeners, which is where the dryness comes from.

name: Angostura Aromatic Bitters
description: Invented in Venezuela in 1824 by a German army surgeon treating stomach complaints, made in Trinidad since 1875, and present behind essentially every bar on earth. The oversized label was a printing error nobody ever corrected.
funFact: The label is famously too big for the bottle because two brothers each did half the job without checking with the other, and the family decided it had become recognisable.

serve.glass: Used as a seasoning, not poured
serve.how: A few dashes into an Old Fashioned, a Manhattan or a Pisco Sour, where it works the way salt works in cooking. Also dashed into soda water for an upset stomach, which was its original purpose.

composition.summary: A concentrated botanical tincture on a high-strength spirit base.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian and a secret blend; despite the name, no angostura bark

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended to a concentrate

composition.process: Only a handful of people know the recipe, and the company keeps them from travelling together.

name: Shrubb
description: Rhum steeped with dried bitter orange peel and spice, made in Martinique and Guadeloupe for Christmas and now sold year-round. Drier and more bitter than any orange liqueur, because the rum underneath is agricole.
funFact: Traditionally the orange peel was dried on rooftops through the year specifically so there would be enough for the Christmas batch.

serve.how: Neat at Christmas, or over ice. It also works in place of curaçao in a Mai Tai, where the agricole base adds a grassy edge that the standard build lacks entirely.

composition.summary: Rhum agricole macerated with bitter orange peel, spice and cane syrup.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sun-dried bitter orange peel, vanilla, clove, cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened with cane syrup

composition.process: Sun-drying the peel concentrates the oil and adds a bitterness fresh peel does not have.

name: Black Seal Rum
description: Bermuda's black rum, blended on the island since 1806 and once sold from the barrel into whatever bottle a customer brought, sealed with black wax. Without it a Dark 'n Stormy is just ginger beer.
funFact: Gosling's holds a trademark on the Dark 'n Stormy, making it one of very few cocktails that legally requires a specific brand.

serve.how: Poured over ginger beer and ice, floated rather than stirred so it sits in a dark layer on top. That is the Dark 'n Stormy, and it is the reason the bottle exists. Neat it is heavy and very sweet.

composition.summary: Caribbean rums blended in Bermuda to a dark house style.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses rums sourced across the Caribbean

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled elsewhere, blended and aged in Bermuda

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Aged in charred American oak before blending

composition.process: Bermuda grows no cane; the island's contribution is the blend, which has stayed in one family for seven generations.

name: Rivers Royale
description: Grenadian cane juice rum at 69 to 75%, made at a distillery that still runs its cane crusher off a water wheel installed in 1785. Raw, hot and utterly uncompromising, and the island drinks it neat.
funFact: River Antoine has been running since 1785 and is widely considered the oldest functioning water-propelled distillery in the Caribbean.

serve.how: Neat in tiny measures, which is how Grenadians take it, or cut heavily with water or coconut water. At 75% it cannot legally be carried on an aircraft, so it is genuinely a drink you have to go there for.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented wild and pot-distilled, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh cane juice from the estate's own fields

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Wood-fired copper pot stills; cane crushed by water wheel

composition.process: Wild fermentation in open stone tanks gives the funk, and the wood fire gives the rest.

name: Nutmeg Liqueur
description: Made from the spice on Grenada's national flag, using both the nutmeg and the red mace that wraps it. The island produces a substantial share of the world's supply and puts it into everything, including this.
funFact: Grenada is the only country whose flag features a food crop, and Hurricane Ivan destroyed around ninety per cent of its nutmeg trees in 2004.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice cream. It also does good work in a rum punch, where a spoonful adds the spice note that grated nutmeg gives on top of the drink.

composition.summary: Nutmeg and mace steeped in rum or neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Nutmeg and its outer mace, plus cane sugar

composition.process: Mace carries a lighter, more floral note than the nut, and using both gives the liqueur its range.

name: Saint Lucian Rum
description: One distillery on the island runs a Coffey still, two pot stills and a John Dore, which gives it more stylistic range than most whole countries manage. The results run from light and clean to thick and estery.
funFact: Saint Lucia Distillers operates four different still types on one site, which is unusual anywhere and rare in the Caribbean.

serve.how: Neat for the aged expressions, which carry real depth. The pot-still-heavy bottlings hold up in a Mai Tai or a Rum Old Fashioned; the lighter ones make excellent daiquiris.

composition.summary: Molasses and cane juice distilled across four still types, then blended.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Coffey still, two pot stills and a John Dore

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, port and sherry casks, tropically aged

composition.process: Having four stills means the blender is building from components rather than adjusting one spirit.

name: English Harbour Rum
description: Antiguan column-still rum, aged beside the old Royal Navy dockyard the brand is named for. Lighter and drier than its neighbours, and the extra-aged releases are among the Caribbean's most underrated bottles.
funFact: English Harbour was Nelson's Caribbean base, and the dockyard is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

serve.how: Neat for anything aged five years and up. The younger expressions mix cleanly with ginger or lime. Tropical ageing means a ten-year-old here has done the work of a much older continental spirit.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented and column-distilled, then tropically aged.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak in tropical conditions, five to twenty-five years

composition.process: Tropical ageing loses far more to evaporation each year, which is why old Caribbean rum is scarce and expensive.

name: Cachaça Envelhecida
description: Aged cachaça, and the reason to take the category seriously. Brazilian producers use native hardwoods — amburana, jequitibá, bálsamo — that give flavours no oak barrel in the world can produce.
funFact: Amburana wood gives a pronounced cinnamon and tonka bean note, which is why aged cachaça often tastes spiced without anything having been added.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, the way you would drink an aged rum. Using a good envelhecida in a caipirinha is not a crime, but the wood notes fight the lime, so the unaged version is better there.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice distilled and aged in Brazilian hardwood casks.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least one year in casks of amburana, jequitibá, bálsamo, ipê or oak

composition.process: Brazilian law recognises around thirty native woods for ageing, each with its own flavour signature.

name: Tiquira
description: Cassava spirit from Maranhão in Brazil's north, made by fermenting the same root that has to be processed carefully to remove its natural cyanide. Sometimes tinted purple by steeping it over a local leaf.
funFact: Indigenous communities in the region were fermenting cassava long before the Portuguese arrived with distilling equipment.

serve.how: Neat and cold in a small glass. It is a regional spirit, rarely found outside Maranhão, and served with the same directness as any village distillate. The purple version is coloured, not flavoured.

composition.summary: Cassava root cooked, fermented and distilled.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, after the starch is converted

composition.process: The root must be cooked thoroughly first, both to convert starch and to drive off its natural toxins.

name: Licor de Jenipapo
description: Genipap liqueur from Brazil's northeast, made from a fruit whose unripe juice stains skin blue-black and was used by indigenous peoples as body paint. Ripe, it makes something dark, sweet and faintly medicinal.
funFact: Jenipapo juice produces a deep blue-black dye on skin that takes over a week to wear off, which is why it was used for ceremonial painting.

serve.how: Cold and neat after a meal. It is thick and sweet, so a small pour is enough. Northeastern Brazilians treat it as a digestive and it appears at festas alongside the local cachaça.

composition.summary: Ripe genipap fruit macerated in cachaça and sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ripe Genipa americana fruit, sugar, sometimes clove

composition.process: Only fully ripe fruit is used; unripe jenipapo is astringent and stains everything it touches.

name: Enguindado
description: Chilean aguardiente steeped with sour cherries, drunk during the September independence celebrations and rarely at any other time. Sweet, red and considerably stronger than the fruit suggests.
funFact: It appears almost exclusively around the Fiestas Patrias in September, alongside the terremoto and chicha that dominate the same week.

serve.how: Cold, in a small glass, with the steeped cherries at the bottom. Chileans drink it at fondas during the September holidays, and the cherries are eaten afterwards.

composition.summary: Sour cherries macerated in aguardiente with sugar.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Guindas, the local sour cherry, plus sugar

composition.process: The cherries keep infusing in the bottle, so a jar opened late in the season is sweeter and deeper.

name: Singani
description: Bolivia's national spirit: Muscat of Alexandria grown above 1,600 metres and distilled to a clear, intensely floral brandy. The altitude stresses the vines, which concentrates the aromatics, and the result tastes like almost nothing else.
funFact: The director Steven Soderbergh discovered it filming in Bolivia and spent years importing it into the United States, where it initially had no legal category to sit in.

serve.how: Chilled and neat, or in a chuflay: singani with ginger ale and lime over ice, which is the Bolivian standard. The floral aroma is the point, so a wine glass serves it better than a shot glass.

composition.summary: High-altitude Muscat of Alexandria fermented and distilled to clear spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Muscat of Alexandria grown above 1,600 metres

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, no water added afterwards

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; rested in steel or glass

composition.process: Bolivian law fixes the minimum altitude, since the vines' response to thin air is what makes the spirit.

name: Viche
description: Artisanal cane spirit from Colombia's Pacific coast, made by Afro-Colombian communities in stills built from whatever is available. Recognised as national cultural patrimony in 2021 after generations of being treated as contraband.
funFact: Viche is the base for a whole family of preparations — arrechón, tomaseca, curao — each traditionally credited with a specific medicinal or restorative purpose.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or in one of its infused forms. Arrechón, blended with milk, honey and herbs, is the best-known preparation and considerably easier going than the raw spirit.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented and distilled in artisanal stills.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; infused versions are common

composition.process: The 2021 law recognising viche was written to protect it as ancestral knowledge, not just as a product.

name: Chirrinchi
description: The Wayúu people's spirit, distilled in the desert of La Guajira on the Colombian and Venezuelan border. Made from panela and used ceremonially as much as socially, in a region where little else grows.
funFact: Chirrinchi is used in Wayúu funerary and negotiation rituals, where offering it carries obligations beyond simple hospitality.

serve.how: Neat in small measures. It is a ceremonial and social spirit within Wayúu communities rather than a bar product, and the commercial bottlings that exist are recent.

composition.summary: Panela fermented and distilled in the Guajira desert.
composition.process: Water is scarce in La Guajira, which shapes both the fermentation and the scale of production.

name: Cocuy
description: Venezuela's agave spirit, made from Agave cocui in Falcón and Lara, and the only agave distillate outside Mexico with a protected denomination. Roasted in earth pits like mezcal, and tasting broadly similar.
funFact: Cocuy was made illegally for most of the twentieth century and only received Venezuelan denomination of origin protection in 2001.

serve.how: Neat and unchilled in a small wide glass, sipped rather than shot, exactly as you would treat mezcal. The wild-harvested versions carry more mineral and less sweetness.

composition.summary: Agave cocui hearts roasted, fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, then small pot stills

composition.process: The plant takes eight to ten years to mature, and overharvesting has been a genuine conservation concern.

name: Pájaro Azul
description: Aguardiente from Ecuador's Bolívar province, infused with herbs and reputedly a few less orthodox ingredients depending on who is making it. Blue bird, in translation, and the name is a warning as much as a brand.
funFact: Guaranda's version is the most famous, and the recipe reportedly varies from producer to producer in ways nobody documents.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, usually at carnival in Guaranda where it is the drink of the festival. It is strong and rough by design, and pacing matters more than technique.

composition.summary: Cane aguardiente infused with herbs and other additions.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Local herbs, anise, and unlisted regional additions

composition.process: Recipes are held locally and vary enough that no two producers make quite the same thing.

name: Grapa Argentina
description: Pomace brandy brought to Argentina by Italian immigrants and made ever since in Mendoza and the wine provinces. Rougher and more rustic than Italian grappa, and drunk in cafés rather than after dinner.
funFact: Italian migration to Argentina was heavy enough that grappa, pizza and a distinct dialect all arrived together and stayed.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, often with coffee. Argentine cafés serve it as a mid-morning fortifier as readily as an after-dinner drink, which is an Italian habit that crossed the Atlantic intact.

composition.summary: Grape pomace from Argentine wine fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pomace from Malbec, Torrontés and other Argentine grapes

composition.process: Mendoza's scale means the pomace supply is enormous, and much of it is distilled rather than composted.

name: Caña
description: Argentine sugarcane spirit, frequently infused with herbs, of which Caña Legui is the name that survives. Once the working drink of the countryside, and still sold with a heavy dose of gaucho nostalgia.
funFact: Caña Legui's advertising has leaned on rural and gaucho imagery for so long that the bottle is a period piece in its own right.

serve.how: Neat, or with a splash of soda. In the countryside it is drunk straight and cold in winter. The herbal versions are sweeter and read closer to a light liqueur than a cane spirit.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit, often infused with herbs and lightly sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Herbs and botanicals in the traditional styles

composition.process: Tucumán and Salta grow the cane, and the spirit was historically a northern rather than a pampas product.

name: Hesperidina
description: A bitter orange-peel aperitif invented in Buenos Aires in 1864 and patented so early that Argentina created a trademark law partly to protect it. Sweeter and gentler than an Italian bitter, and unmistakably Argentine.
funFact: Melville Sewell Bagley registered it in 1876 as Argentina's first trademark, having built anticipation by chalking the single word Hesperidina on walls across the city before launch.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and an orange slice, which is the standard Buenos Aires aperitif serve. It also works in place of sweet vermouth in a spritz, being lower in alcohol and higher in orange.

composition.summary: Bitter orange peel macerated in spirit, sweetened and rested.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bitter orange peel, herbs and spices

composition.process: The wall-chalking campaign that launched it is credited as one of the first modern teaser advertisements anywhere.

name: Grappamiel
description: Uruguayan grappa cut with honey, which turns a rough pomace spirit into something warming and easy. Drunk through the winter and sold in every Uruguayan supermarket alongside the yerba mate.
funFact: Uruguay's Italian-descended population is proportionally even larger than Argentina's, which is why grappa took root there so completely.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, or warmed slightly in winter. Uruguayans drink it against the cold coming off the Río de la Plata, and it does the job. Also good poured into coffee.

composition.summary: Grape pomace spirit blended with honey.
composition.process: The honey rounds off the pomace spirit's edges without disguising it entirely.

name: Caña Paraguaya
description: Paraguay's national spirit, distilled from sugarcane grown across the country and drunk in enormous quantity. Often aged in native woods, which gives it colour and a distinctly local spice.
funFact: Paraguayans mix it with coconut water and lemon to make caribe, a drink that is close to a national institution during Carnival.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or mixed into caribe with coconut water and lime. Aged versions in native hardwood are worth drinking on their own and are increasingly bottled for export.

composition.summary: Paraguayan sugarcane fermented and distilled, sometimes wood-aged.
composition.process: Paraguay grows a great deal of organic cane, much of which goes into caña rather than sugar.

name: Borgoe
description: Surinamese rum, made in the only Dutch-speaking country in South America from cane grown along the coastal plain. Light, clean and almost entirely unknown outside the Netherlands and the Guianas.
funFact: Suriname's distillery draws on a sugar industry that dates to Dutch plantation agriculture in the seventeenth century.

serve.how: Over ice with cola or soda, which is how it is drunk in Paramaribo and Amsterdam alike. The aged expressions take a single cube neat and carry more vanilla than the age statement suggests.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented and column-distilled, then oak-aged.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, from one to eight years

composition.process: Most of the output goes to the Netherlands, where the Surinamese diaspora keeps the brand alive.
